reasoning_traces.think:
The primary mechanism of behavioral learning involves reinforcement gradients that are susceptible to interference from secondary stimuli. The false reinforcement (R_f) initially biases learning toward incorrect paths, slowing convergence. Extinction effects propagate from incorrect to correct choices through a generalized kernel (K), weakening the latter and further retarding progress. Spatial orientation (S_o) introduces another layer of complexity, where organisms attempt to return to reinforcement points, but only within a limited range. When this constraint is violated, learning degrades. These three phenomena form a triadic system where each component interacts with the others—interference affects gradient steepness, extinction modifies the signal-to-noise ratio, and spatial constraints limit the effective domain of reinforcement. The combined effect is a degradation of learning efficiency that manifests as increased time to convergence and reduced accuracy. This can be modeled as a coupled dynamical system with feedback loops between reinforcement, extinction, and spatial memory. The failure modes include: (1) high R_f leading to persistent false learning, (2) strong K causing overgeneralization, and (3) weak S_o resulting in navigation inefficiency. Each mode contributes to a degradation of the learning signal, ultimately reducing the efficacy of the behavioral adaptation process.
